source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources (see each document’s sourcing note)

books.section: America Transformed into the Industrial Giant

primary_sources: Udo J. Keppler, “The New South — The Triumph of Free Labor,” Puck (1895)
Booker T. Washington, address at the Atlanta Cotton States and International Exposition (1895)
W. E. B. Du Bois, “Strivings of the Negro People” (1897)

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the South changed in the period 1865–1898.

documents.title: Grady’s “New South”
documents.source: Henry W. Grady, “The New South,” address to the New England Society of New York, December 1886. Public domain.
documents.text: “There was a South of slavery and secession — that South is dead. There is a South of union and freedom — that South, thank God, is living, breathing, growing every hour.” . . . “The old South rested everything on slavery and agriculture, unconscious that these could neither give nor maintain healthy growth. The new South presents a perfect democracy, the oligarchs leading in the popular movement; a social system compact and closely knitted, less splendid on the surface, but stronger at the core; a hundred farms for every plantation, fifty homes for every palace; and a diversified industry that meets the complex needs of this complex age.”
documents.sourcing: Grady, an Atlanta editor, speaking to Northern businessmen; his purpose is to win their investment by promising a reconciled, industrial South.

documents.title: The New South — The Triumph of Free Labor
documents.source: Udo J. Keppler, “The New South — The Triumph of Free Labor,” Puck magazine, October 23, 1895. Public domain (Library of Congress).
documents.text: A large Black worker wearing a sash reading “FREE LABOR” stands with a hammer in one hand and a plow at his feet. Behind him, a crowd of Black and white Southerners, including Civil War veterans, walks past a statue of Abraham Lincoln toward a bright fairground. A flag reads “ATLANTA EXPOSITION,” and the word “PROSPERITY” shines in the sky above the fairground.
documents.sourcing: A Northern magazine cartoon celebrating the Atlanta Exposition; its purpose is to sell the New South as free labor’s triumph to a national audience.

documents.title: A sharecropping contract
documents.source: Sharecropping contract, De Soto County, Mississippi, 1867. Salisbury University, Nabb Research Center. Public domain.
documents.text: The title page of a sharecropping contract from De Soto County, Mississippi, dated 1867. Sharecropping contracts bound freedmen to work a landowner’s fields for a year and pay rent with a share of the crop, while buying supplies on credit from the landowner.
documents.sourcing: A labor contract between a landowner and freedmen, showing the terms on which freedpeople worked the land after emancipation.

documents.title: The Atlanta Compromise
documents.source: Booker T. Washington, address at the Atlanta Cotton States and International Exposition, September 18, 1895. Public domain.
documents.text: “Cast down your bucket where you are.” . . . “In all things that are purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress.”
documents.sourcing: Washington, the leading Black spokesman of the day, addressing a mostly white Southern audience; his purpose is to offer a bargain of economic cooperation in exchange for tolerance.

documents.title: Plessy v. Ferguson
documents.source: Plessy v. Ferguson, 163 U.S. 537 (1896). Majority opinion by Justice Henry Billings Brown. Public domain.
documents.text: “We consider the underlying fallacy of the plaintiff’s argument to consist in the assumption that the enforced separation of the two races stamps the colored race with a badge of inferiority. If this be so, it is not by reason of anything found in the act, but solely because the colored race chooses to put that construction upon it.”
documents.sourcing: The Supreme Court majority ruling on Louisiana’s Separate Car Act; its reasoning gave segregation the cover of law.

documents.title: Southern Horrors
documents.source: Ida B. Wells, Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases (1892), quoting her editorial in the Memphis Free Speech, May 21, 1892. Public domain.
documents.text: “Eight negroes lynched since last issue of the Free Speech, one at Little Rock, Ark., . . . and five on the same old racket — the new alarm about raping white women. The same programme of hanging, then shooting bullets into the lifeless bodies was carried out to the letter. Nobody in this section of the country believes the old thread-bare lie that Negro men rape white women.”
documents.sourcing: Wells, a Black journalist whose Memphis newspaper was destroyed for this editorial; her purpose is to expose lynching as terror, not punishment.

documents.title: Strivings of the Negro People
documents.source: W. E. B. Du Bois, “Strivings of the Negro People,” Atlantic Monthly, August 1897. Public domain.
documents.text: “It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one’s self through the eyes of others, of measuring one’s soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity. One ever feels his two-ness, — an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder.”
documents.sourcing: Du Bois, a young Black scholar writing for a Northern magazine audience; his purpose is to describe what it feels like to be Black in a Jim Crow nation.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The South changed in real ways between 1865 and 1898 — new mills, cities, and a free-labor economy replaced slavery — but the change was partial, because white supremacy was rebuilt through sharecropping, segregation, disenfranchisement, and terror, so the New South was new in its industry and old in its racial order.

Economic change: Grady’s promise of diversified industry (Doc 1) and the Keppler cartoon’s celebration of free labor (Doc 2) show a South selling itself as industrial and modern.

Economic continuity: the sharecropping contract (Doc 3) shows freedpeople still working white-owned land and paying rent with the crop, so the labor system echoed slavery’s dependence.

Racial order: Washington’s bargain of economic cooperation (Doc 4), the Plessy ruling blessing separation (Doc 5), Wells’s account of lynching as terror (Doc 6), and Du Bois’s double-consciousness (Doc 7) show Black Southerners negotiating, enduring, and naming a system built to keep them second-class.

Outside evidence: the Compromise of 1877 and the withdrawal of federal troops, the Mississippi constitution of 1890 and the collapse of Black voter registration, and the growth of Southern textile mills and Birmingham steel.

Complexity: change and continuity ran together — the economy industrialized in pockets while the racial order hardened, so the New South was both a real break from the plantation past and a rebuilding of white supremacy in new forms.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the South changed between 1865 and 1898, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the Civil War and emancipation, Reconstruction and its end in 1877, or the rise of industrial America.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument about change in the South.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Compromise of 1877, the Mississippi constitution of 1890, the collapse of Black voter registration, or the growth of Southern textile mills.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document’s author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least three documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing fewer than three documents, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, explaining why change was uneven, or showing that different groups experienced the New South differently.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.
